R_H1.passageTitle: How a Large City Helps People Find Their Way

passages.label: A
passages.text: How can someone find the right station without being an expert in Tokyo's place names? In Japan's capital, a modern city with a very large population, a letter and a number can make an unfamiliar train journey easier to organise. Road traffic can slow a visitor on the way to the city centre. Streets near major roads may be noisy, and this makes the train an interesting alternative for people who want to reach another area.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Tokyo Metro is one part of the city's transport system. Its nine subway lines take people to different parts of the city. Local people may know their stations by name, while visitors often need another way to recognise a stop. Sometimes a person plans a journey to a quiet area away from a road. First they need to know how to tell which stations are on their route.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Every Metro station has a code that includes a letter for the line and a number for the station, and this helps a visitor recognise a stop even if the place name sounds strange. Large stations can be crowded, and a journey may start near an apartment in an urban district and end beside a popular museum, bridge or lake. The same method of using codes is useful for travellers with different destinations.

passages.label: D
passages.text: To plan a transfer, find the letter for the initial line, then look up the station number. A passenger can follow the numbers toward the transfer station and count how many stops there are before it. A change in the letter at the interchange identifies a different line, allowing passengers to distinguish the next direction of travel from the destination on their first train. In a crowded interchange, the station number is an additional reference when a passenger is comparing signs on different platforms or checking an announcement about the next service. Check where the platform is located before you change lines. A display may show a different exit towards a residential street than towards a beautiful public garden.

passages.label: E
passages.text: The official map and the Metro website allow passengers to identify a station by name or number. The Fare and Transfer Search gives the fare for a destination, so someone can compare a cheap trip with a more expensive option. This does not depend on whether a place is quiet or whether the streets nearby are clean, and the labels have a more specific purpose. They are an opportunity to divide an unfamiliar journey into a sequence of smaller decisions, and an English map can also be saved before leaving. That helps when a person needs to check a number while standing on the platform.

R_H2.passageTitle: A Large City's Shared Green Space

passages.label: A
passages.text: A noisy road in a modern capital can be only a short walk from a quiet place. Hyde Park covers 350 acres near the city centre of London, where the population and traffic are large. Its paths and water give local people a different kind of area to use, and a beautiful place in a city can also be a place where people do very ordinary things.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Hyde Park was originally royal hunting land, and that use changed when King Charles I opened it to the public in 1637. Opening the grounds made later gatherings possible, including the Great Exhibition of 1851, when a site that had been set aside for royal use became a setting for a major public event. The park is located in central London, where open space is shared by residents and visitors.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The Courts, on the south side of the park, offer sports such as tennis to people at different levels of experience. Residents and visitors choose an activity and pay for it, and advance booking is advisable because the facilities are popular. In this way, sporting opportunities remain available within a central part of the city, and the attraction for some people is the game, while others come to walk or sit. The same land can serve both purposes at once.

passages.label: D
passages.text: The Serpentine is a popular lake, and a visitor can recognise the western end by a bridge and see how the water lies between buildings and open grass. At a crowded time, someone from an apartment can still find an open field or a path near the woods. Places like this add room for outdoor activity in an urban district.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Reeds, tall plants that grow by water, stand along parts of the Serpentine. Their roots help clean the water, while their leaves give cover to some of the birds that nest there, and an interesting thing about this corner of London is how many uses can sit together. A visitor may see a swan while someone else uses the paths to get exercise, and there is even an opportunity to pause and watch the insects and small creatures that live near the water. The park gives wildlife a place in a city affected by pollution. Roads elsewhere may be polluted and busy, while the park gives a person room to stop. London City Hall points to the way parks allow people to walk, cycle and meet each other, and a large city can make space for all of these uses in the same public area.

R_H3.passageTitle: A Homestay in Victoria: More than a Room

passages.label: A
passages.text: When students choose a homestay in Victoria, the question is what life in the home will include. Victoria is the capital of British Columbia in Canada. At the University of Victoria, international students can live with a Canadian family and use English in real situations, and it is one opportunity to get to know a local area. A view of beautiful countryside or a visit to a modern city centre can be interesting, but home life will also involve daily tasks.

passages.label: B
passages.text: A host family provides a private furnished bedroom, meals, internet access and laundry access. Host homes have access to regular bus routes, and these details help a new student manage everyday life. A bedroom can be a quiet place for homework, and a bus route helps a student travel between home and the university.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Before students arrive, families apply to the programme, and staff meet and interview them in their homes. Staff check that each home is safe and meets programme requirements, and the programme gives hosts information and support. A homestay is more than an empty bedroom: the host family and student will share a home, so both need to understand the arrangement.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Before accepting an offer, look at where the home is located, and a house near the woods in a rural area can mean a long trip into the city. An apartment in an urban district may be easier to reach by a popular bus, although the route might be crowded at busy times. A bridge, a lake or an open field can help a student recognise places on a map and understand how far the home is from class. A map also makes it easier to ask a host about travel.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Students should keep their room clean and let the family know when they will be late. They prepare their breakfast and lunch from food the family provides and look after their own washing. A family in a quiet area may live farther from some activities. A home near noisy traffic may make a journey shorter, but the student still needs to check bus routes. Some homes are closer to the city centre than to the countryside. The programme lists what is included, such as meals, internet access and laundry. A room that seems cheap can be more expensive to live in if the student needs to pay for other things. This is why students compare the whole arrangement and ask what they will have to do themselves before deciding.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: What does the opening suggest living with a family can add to a visit to the area?
options: It takes away the need to organise ordinary tasks or use the local language.
It is mainly a way to avoid contact with people who live in the area.
It can provide a way to use English in real situations while taking part in daily home life.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: What kind of help with daily travel is stated for the host homes?
options: A guarantee that every host will drive students wherever they want.
Access to regular bus routes that can help students get between home and class.
A condition that every bedroom is located on the campus.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: What is the purpose of learning about a household before a placement goes ahead?
options: The programme can use what it learns to check the home and prepare people for a shared arrangement.
The programme can decide which guest will be allowed to keep the furniture after leaving.
The household is only being checked for how close it is to every place of interest.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: What comparison does the text make between homes in less urban and more urban areas?
options: A house near woods necessarily has the shortest journey into the city.
Going by city bus guarantees a quiet trip at all times.
A home farther out can take longer to reach, while an urban bus can be easier to reach but busy.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why can recognising a bridge or lake on a map be useful before taking an offer?
options: It can help a student place the home relative to classes and ask the host about travel.
It tells the student exactly how much will be charged for every household service.
It means asking about available buses is no longer needed.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: One option takes more travelling but feels peaceful. Another is nearer busy roads but shortens the journey. How should the student decide?
options: Let a calm setting decide and assume the time spent travelling will not matter.
Consider what it is like at the home and how the commute would really work.
Choose by the size of the road without finding out whether it connects to class.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: How are food arrangements divided between a host and the person staying?
options: The student needs to buy and cook all food independently of the host.
Meals being listed means the student is never expected to make anything to eat.
The host provides food, and the student prepares some meals from what is provided.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: What everyday responsibility does the guide name for use of the student’s room?
options: Ask the host to do the student’s clothes washing whenever needed.
Stop using the room whenever the family is preparing food.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why might the room that first looks cheapest cost more once a student lives there?
options: People always have to pay the same amount regardless of what is included.
Other things the student needs may have to be paid for separately.
Living near a bus means the host no longer needs to provide a bedroom.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: What should someone compare before accepting a homestay offer?
options: How modern each bedroom looks as the only guide to daily life.
The size of the city and which home is nearest to a public attraction, leaving out other arrangements.
What comes with the room, how the student will travel, and what they must do or pay for themselves.
